1:
Henry will not let the objection stand as it reads. It contradicts what God had just said, that they would hearken to his voice; and if God says they will, it does not become Moses to say they will not, so Henry supposes he meant that perhaps they would not at first, or some of them would not. Ellicott denies him the escape: some do render the opening word perhaps, but it bears that meaning nowhere, and Moses expressed a settled conviction that he would not be listened to. Ellicott concedes the fear was reasonable, there having been no appearance of God for four hundred years, and generalises it: miracles cluster about certain crises in God’s dealings and cease altogether between them, as they were suspended for five centuries between Daniel and the angel who came to Zacharias. Calvin traces the hesitation to timidity rather than stubbornness: Moses does not shake off the yoke as an unruly beast does but shrinks from it, and though he neither disbelieved the promise nor wished to refuse the burden, the sight of dangers left his mind a prey to conflicting feelings — a state no believer escapes when obstacles darken his mind. Henry adds that those whom God designs for preferment He first clothes with humility, and that good men sometimes think worse of people than they deserve, the chapter ending by saying the people believed.

What the rod was they cannot agree. Clarke takes it for a staff and probably a shepherd’s crook, later called the rod of God. Keil and Delitzsch make the crook the point of the sign: it stood for the calling Moses was asked to give up. But more is meant, since the serpent had been the enemy of the seed of the woman and stood for the evil power prevailing in Egypt; they cite a rabbinic comment that as the serpent bites and kills, so Pharaoh and the Egyptians bit and killed Israel. Calvin works the image the other way: nothing could be more contemptible than a shepherd coming out of the desert to set against a king’s sceptre a stick with which he could hardly defend his flock — yet turned into a serpent it would inspire more terror than a thousand swords. Ellicott dissents. Most commentators say a shepherd’s crook and it is possible, but the etymology points rather to an ordinary walking-stick, and he settles for a common staff such as a man of eighty might want for support.

Clarke and Ellicott agree that the Hebrew word is generic and names no species; Clarke supposes a kind Moses had not seen or one he knew dangerous, since he fled. Calvin reads the flight as deliberate: God meant to frighten His servant so that Moses might judge from his own alarm what the same power would do to the proud king. Gill explains the command to seize the tail as given partly so Moses might know it a real serpent, partly to try his courage, and reports a comment that the head belonged not to Moses but to Christ, who was speaking from the bush. Ellicott observes that snake-handlers take them by the neck where they cannot bite, so the order was a test; faith triumphed over instinct. Clarke draws the moral that obedience conquers all difficulties.

The sentence about believing breaks off unfinished, as Clarke and Wesley both note, and both supply the same words. Ellicott finds in it a divine sanction for the view, strangely resisted of late, that miracles are given primarily for their evidential value, to accredit God’s messengers; without them neither would Moses have persuaded Israel nor the apostles converted the world. Gill insists the sign was not for Moses at all, whose faith the burning bush had settled, but for Israel. Calvin says miracles serve sometimes to prepare faith and sometimes to confirm it, and finds both here.
6:
Clarke describes the disease as thin white scales spreading over the whole body, and quotes a physician who had seen a man whose skin shone as though covered with snow. Among the Jews it was reckoned incurable; among the heathen it was thought inflicted by the gods and removable only by them, and Clarke finds the same belief in Israel, since the king rent his clothes when Naaman was sent to him and asked whether he was God, to kill and to make alive. That, he concludes, is why the sign was chosen: the instant infliction and removal of such a disease was a demonstration everyone would allow of God’s sovereign power, and no other reason need be sought. Ellicott adds that the worst form, called by the Greeks the white disease, turns the skin glossy white and every hair white like wool, and was held absolutely incurable; and he suggests that it may have been from Moses exhibiting a leprous hand that Egyptian writers came to call the Israelites the lepers.

Where Clarke forbids further reasons, the others supply them. Calvin takes the sign to teach that whatever is at its greatest vigour withers at once at God’s word, and what is dry is restored, confirming Paul’s saying that God calls the things that are not as though they were. He then applies it to Moses himself: it was a kind of leprosy when he was banished from the court into Midian, and after forty years passed like a man half dead he recovered what he had lost as by a restoration. All men, he adds, stand or fall at God’s will, and their strength fails suddenly when they seem strongest. Wesley reads the sign forward instead of backward: Moses would bring sore diseases on Egypt and remove them at his prayer, and Israel, grown leprous with sin and nearly consumed by oppression, would be cleansed by being taken into his bosom.

Ellicott presses the phrase about the voice of the sign: it means not the voice of Moses attested by the sign but the voice the sign itself utters, as the psalm speaks of Moses and Aaron proclaiming the words of God’s signs. He then explains the ascending order: the Israelites were used to serpent-charmers and might be unmoved by the first wonder, while the second had no parallel in their experience; and because some might still doubt, a third was provided, for God is patient with all reasonable doubt. Clarke says the same briefly, and Wesley draws the lesson that God’s works have a voice we must diligently observe. Calvin reads the accumulation as longsuffering: those who neglected the first miracle were unworthy of a second, and to persevere in arresting their dullness was a wonderful clemency — the same by which God still adds new remedies for the cure of our unbelief. Gill notes that the first two signs were repeated before the people in Egypt.

Keil and Delitzsch make the third sign a practical demonstration of the power Moses had received over the might and the gods of Egypt, water being taken from the Nile itself and poured on dry ground. Calvin presses it harder: the first two showed the power that would work by Moses’s hand, but this taught what God’s dealings with Egypt would be, so that the very strongholds they trusted in — and they drew many advantages from the river — would be found against them. Ellicott observes that the Hebrew repeats the verb, intensifying it to shall assuredly become, and reads all three signs together: chosen for ease of exhibition, each may also be significant — the rod showing that a feeble implement can become a power to chastise, the hand made leprous and clean indicating a mission both to punish and to save, and the water turned to blood hinting at the conversion of Egypt’s prosperity into bloodshed.
10:
What the defect was, none of them can say. Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase as meaning that Moses lacked the gift of speech and found a difficulty in the use of mouth and tongue, and expressly deny that it was stammering; he had neither the gift by nature nor received it since God began to speak with him. Ellicott reports a Jewish tradition that he could not pronounce the labials, and adds that converse with God had not cured the impediment, whatever it was. Clarke faces the harder problem, that Stephen calls Moses mighty in words, and offers three solutions: an infirmity he afterwards overcame; an imperfect command of Hebrew after forty years at the Egyptian court and forty in Midian; or a man slow of speech yet mighty in word as God’s messenger, since at his command the plagues came and were stayed. Gill reaches the third of these from the promise that follows.

Henry and Wesley give the same account of the man in almost the same words: a great philosopher, statesman and divine, yet no orator, of a clear head and solid judgment but without a voluble tongue; what he said was strong and to the purpose and distilled as the dew, though he did not deliver it with the readiness of others. Henry alone draws the inferences: we must not judge men by fluency, since Paul’s speech was called contemptible and much wisdom hides behind a slow tongue, and God sometimes chooses messengers with the fewest natural advantages so that His grace may appear the more — Christ’s disciples were no orators until the Spirit made them so. Calvin reaches the same conclusion independently: the least suitable instruments are the ones God especially employs, that His power may more fully appear, and He could have made Moses eloquent from the womb. But Calvin also weighs the fault. Moses catches at every word of escape, not from a wish to refuse but from trembling at the task, and his error was in not casting his care on God and hoping against hope as Abraham did. To reflect on his own defect was modesty, had he gone on to ask for help; to ask instead to be discharged was to do God an injustice. It is lawful to fear in perplexities, so long as the anxiety does not overcome the desire to obey; but no pretext makes it right to refuse what God enjoins.

The answer turns on who made the mouth. Gill takes it that the God who put the faculty of speech into the first man can remove any impediment; Clarke turns it into a warning, since He who created the eye and the ear also made the blind and the deaf; Keil and Delitzsch say He holds unlimited power over all the senses; Ellicott corrects only the tense, that the verb should be hath made. Calvin builds the largest structure on it. Since God alone governs the tongue He created, the difference between the tongueless and the eloquent is of His good pleasure, from which it follows that all nature lies under His government. More than that, eloquence is a matter of special grace, and it remains in His hand to strike the most fluent dumb and to fit the tongue of the dumb for speech; experience confirms it, since those who excel in readiness sometimes want words, while the slow of speech will plead one cause with admirable dexterity.

On the promise to be with his mouth, Clarke records that the Aramaic versions render it of the Word of God being with his speech, and Ellicott glosses it as suggesting words and assisting utterance. Keil and Delitzsch see the significance of the point reached: every difficulty Moses had raised was now answered, and what remained came out next as the real reason, that he simply did not wish to undertake the mission.
13:
The request has been read as a prayer for the Messiah, and two voices reject it. Clarke reports many taking Moses to be asking for the immediate mission of Christ, and answers that while it is right to find the Messiah wherever he is really mentioned, to press into that service passages with no obvious tendency that way is improper and dangerous; Moses, he is firmly of opinion, had no reference to the Messiah here, and God would hardly have been angry at such a request. Calvin gives the same verdict for the same reason: the christological reading is forced and contradicted by the context, since God would not have been roused to anger by such a prayer. He also rejects the reading that makes the phrase mean Aaron, taking it as asking that God direct whomever He pleases — anyone else at all. Ellicott has no patience with it: the sentence means simply pray send by whom thou wilt, and is curt and scarcely reverent. Gill alone hears the opposite tone, taking the opening words to mean that the blame or burden may be laid on Moses himself.

How the anger showed itself Gill cannot decide, listing four possibilities: the impediment not removed, the priesthood withheld, his honour lessened by a partner, or his exclusion from Canaan. He adds that Moses proves himself a faithful historian by recording his own weakness. Wesley draws the moral that self-distrust, when it grows to an extreme and clogs us in duty, is very displeasing to God. Calvin makes the verse a proof that there is no better sacrifice than obedience: God had pardoned the slowness, but when Moses obstinately refused He spared him no longer, and we should beware of taking forbearance for permission to abuse it — though it is fatherly kindness that His anger contents itself with a reproof. He then asks whether Aaron had been chosen from the first or conceded to Moses’s diffidence, and prefers the second: Aaron was added in anger and part of the honour transferred to him.

Ellicott asks why Aaron is called the Levite: the usual explanation, that it distinguished him from others of the name, is superfluous beside "thy brother", so it is probably a title of honour. He and Clarke agree that the doubled Hebrew verb means facility of utterance rather than excellence. Keil and Delitzsch reconcile Aaron’s coming to meet Moses with the later verse where God directs him: he set out of his own accord and was then shown the road. Clarke thinks the assurance was needed against any suspicion of an elder brother’s envy.

On the division of labour they agree. Ellicott notes that God spoke to Aaron only through Moses, so that Aaron was to treat what Moses told him as coming from God, and Moses kept the higher place. Calvin puts it that Moses has the authority and Aaron the interpretation, and finds in the subordination of the firstborn a witness that gifts and vocations are distributed at God’s good pleasure, and a judgment we should reverence because it is past finding out. Wesley adds that even Aaron could not speak to purpose unless God were with his mouth. On the rod, Calvin and Wesley converge: it was the shepherd’s crook, carried so that Moses should not be ashamed of the mean condition out of which God called him, the badge of a rustic occupation set against Pharaoh’s sceptre — God hides His treasures in earthen vessels. Wesley adds that it was to be to him instead of both sword and sceptre. Clarke goes off in another direction, arguing that the thyrsus of Bacchus and the caduceus of Mercury are borrowed from this rod, and that the poets’ Bacchus — exposed on the Nile, a lawgiver with laws on two tables and a serpent-wreathed staff — is a copy of Moses.
18:
That Moses asked leave at all pleases Henry: the honour of communion with God does not exempt a man from the duties of his family and calling. That he asked without mentioning the vision divides them. Henry sets it down to reticence, such favours being for thanksgiving and not for boasting. Clarke rejects that account: Moses was truly humble, but prudence alone explains it, since news told in Midian might reach Egypt before he did, and rumour would have made him out to be coming to stir sedition. Calvin finds the silence surprising, since the vision was the very thing that would have moved Jethro to consent; he cannot decide whether Moses was forbidden by God or held back by fear, and inclines to think he dared not speak of a call so incredible that he would be suspected of falsehood and vanity, putting forward a natural affection as his pretext. Ellicott takes a fourth line: the reason given was true though not the chief one, and Moses was within his right in stating it and leaving the rest unmentioned. He adds that marriage had probably adopted Moses into the tribe, so leave was proper, and that the word rendered brethren means his kith and kin.

Calvin turns the episode into a lesson about reputation: Jethro was persuaded more by divine prompting than by the excuse, but forty years of proven honesty had put Moses past suspicion. Ellicott draws a portrait of Jethro instead: a second Melchizedek, priest and king, in whose presence both Moses and Aaron take second place, yet who never asserts himself. Clarke notes that the Greek and Coptic add a sentence about the death of the king of Egypt, judging it a marginal note crept into the text.

The word coming to Moses in Midian raises a question of order. Calvin holds that what was omitted earlier is inserted here out of place, things not always being recorded in Scripture in the order they happened. Keil and Delitzsch reject both that and the alternative, refusing to make the verse a summary of the earlier revelation and equally refusing to treat it as another writer’s account placing the summons in Midian. Ellicott suggests Moses delayed after getting permission, which is why the command is peremptory, and identifies those who sought his life as Pharaoh, the kindred of the man he killed and the officers charged to arrest him. Henry and Calvin agree on why the assurance mattered: some secret fear of falling into their hands probably lay under all the objections Moses had raised. Calvin adds that Jethro must long since have asked why Moses was a fugitive, so that in reporting a safe return promised by revelation he told no falsehood. Wesley calls it a second vision.

On the journey they pause over the single beast. Clarke notes that the Greek reads asses in the plural, one animal being unable to carry Zipporah and two boys; Ellicott allows either, a singular with the article sometimes standing for the kind. Keil and Delitzsch keep the one ass for the wife and children while Moses walks with the staff of God in his hand, observing that poor as his appearance was, he carried the staff before which all Pharaoh’s pride would bow. Calvin makes the same contrast: the ass proves how slender his substance was, and he did not scruple to appear in the dress in which his poverty would now be conspicuous — a heavy temptation withstood, the poor being driven to crime more by shame than by hunger. Having the rod, he could dispense with the pomp of royalty. Ellicott calls the title emphatic, the endowment of the staff with miraculous power having made it God’s; Wesley and Clarke say the same of the crook that would now rule Israel; and Gill reads the taking of wife and sons as proof that Moses meant to stay.
21:
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that the wonders are not the three signs already given but the whole series to be worked before Pharaoh. Calvin sees why the warning was needed: without it Moses might have thrown away his rod when two or three miracles failed, so God exhorts him to persevere, forewarning that the contest will be long so that the victory may be the more splendid.

The hardening of Pharaoh’s heart is the crux, and every voice handles it differently. Clarke admits the case has produced fierce controversy, then cites Augustine: God hardens not by infusing malice but by withholding mercy, and may be said to harden the man He declines to soften. It is just that graces often offered and despised be at last withheld. He then notes that the Hebrew literally means to strengthen or embolden, a verb written by the Jews at the close of most biblical books to hearten the reader. Ellicott builds a developmental account. The hardening is ascribed variously to God, to Pharaoh and to the heart itself; these may be three ways of saying one thing or three operations, and he prefers the second, each expression having a period in which it predominates. At first Pharaoh was unimpressed, and his heart is said to have hardened itself; then he was impressed but by an effort of will determined not to yield; and only after he had twice done so did God step in and smite him with blindness as a judgment. Wesley states the same sequence but names another agent: after Pharaoh has often hardened it himself, God will at last permit Satan to harden it effectually. Calvin allows none of these softenings: God declares Himself the moderator of the whole contest, so that whatever seemed to oppose the deliverance arose from His own secret counsel; the king was not obstinate against God’s will, but was hardened so that he might be the more violently overwhelmed.

On the title given to Israel they divide as sharply. Clarke glosses it as meaning that the Hebrew people are unutterably dear to God, and Wesley likewise as precious and honourable, adding that this is the first time the formula thus saith the Lord is used by any man. Ellicott denies exactly that reading: the relation is now first revealed and is not a metaphor meaning as dear to me as a son but a reality, the Israel of God enjoying the sonship of adoption by being taken into the True Son. Keil and Delitzsch ground the sonship in election from the call of Abraham, the nation being called son here though only at Sinai made the people of possession. Calvin reads the words as a legal answer to Pharaoh’s only defence. Jacob had brought his family under Egyptian government of his own accord, so by the law of nations the king held them lawfully; God therefore pleads the privilege exempting this people, since it would be absurd that the Maker of heaven and earth be robbed of sons He had adopted. Calvin then guards it: this is not to be extended to believers generally, as though it were wrong for them to be subject to kings, or as though temporal subjection cost them their inheritance.

The threat against Pharaoh’s firstborn, Calvin observes, was not the opening of the embassy but its last clause, delivered when all else had been tried; the instruction now given was to steel Moses for a denunciation sure to rouse the tyrant’s anger. Ellicott says the same: the threat is not uttered until just before the tenth plague, the later speech being much abbreviated. Clarke explains why the service could not be rendered in Egypt, the animals to be sacrificed being sacred to the Egyptians. Gill notes that the saying is a command, and Wesley closes plainly: as men deal with God’s people, let them expect the like themselves.
24:
Henry calls this a very difficult passage, and everyone treats it so. The sin is agreed: the circumcision of a son had been neglected. Henry and Wesley explain it in almost the same words, as the effect of an unequal marriage with a Midianite too indulgent of her child while Moses was too indulgent of her, and both remark that God had lately conversed with him as a friend and now came as an enemy. Henry warns that fondness for any relation may prevail above our love to God, and lays down that omissions are sins which come into judgment, neglect of the covenant seals especially: a man who will not seal a bargain may be suspected of neither liking it nor meaning to stand to it.

Who was in danger is disputed. Gill says plainly that it was Moses and not the child, and rejects the explanations that make the offence bringing his family or lingering at the inn. Clarke takes precisely the reading Gill refuses: the words about slaying a firstborn were spoken not to Pharaoh but to Moses about Gershom, and the threat fell on the child who stood outside the covenant. How the attack came is disputed too. Ellicott says God visited Moses with an illness that threatened to be fatal, and prefers the Hebrew to the versions reading an angel of the Lord. Calvin rebukes exactly that confidence: the phrase means an adverse encounter, in what form we do not know, and those who call the scourge a disease speak too boldly — as do the rabbis who make the offence consist in taking the family along. It is enough that Moses was terrified and shown the cause, since neither he nor his wife would otherwise have thought of circumcising the child. Ellicott adds that there would have been no inn in that country, only a recognised halting-place.

Ellicott notes that stone knives were used by the Egyptian embalmers and reckoned purer than metal, and that Israel still used them in Joshua’s day; Gill adds that the Jewish canons allow a woman to perform the rite. What Zipporah meant by casting it down divides them. Ellicott has no doubt the feet were Moses’s and the act petulant: she thought the rites of her husband’s religion barbarous, and threw the foreskin at him as at a Moloch demanding blood. Gill rejects the readings that put the feet at the child’s or make the phrase mean blood running down. Calvin is more interested in the irregularity. Some rabbis suppose she acted in her husband’s absence, but the context forbids it; she caught up a stone in the haste of fear. The child was certainly not duly circumcised, and yet the event proves that the rite so rashly performed pleased God — not that imperfect obedience pleases Him absolutely, but by indulgence it is sometimes accepted. We must not make it an example, as though hypocrites showing signs of repentance would always find God merciful.

Gill takes it that the Lord let Moses go, and dismisses as ungrammatical the construction that would make Zipporah the one who departed; Ellicott says God accepted her act as sufficient though tardy reparation. Keil and Delitzsch treat the episode as a lesson Moses had to learn before executing his commission, that a man must first prove a faithful servant in his own house, the token of favour following at once in the coming of Aaron. Ellicott supposes that when Moses recovered Zipporah explained her phrase as meant of the two circumcisions together, Gershom’s years before and this one now, and that she and the boys were sent back to Jethro. Wesley reaches the same conclusion less charitably, that she would not let the reproach drop — whatever is likely to hinder us in a special service for God should be removed as far as we can.
27:
How Aaron knew where to go is left open. Clarke supposes some secret movement on his mind, or a voice or angelic ministry, and marvels that both were informed so exactly that they reached the mountain together. Ellicott reasons that the directions must have been fuller than the words recorded, or supplemented on the way, since left to himself Aaron would have looked for his brother in Midian. Calvin attends to what the command does not say. After so long a silence Aaron must have supposed his brother dead in exile; yet God says nothing about the deliverance, and simply requires the elder brother to become the disciple of the younger. For all his promptitude Aaron is not put on an equality with Moses, who is slow and vacillating and almost supine, but is told to learn the design of God from him. From this Calvin draws his point: though Aaron was God’s messenger and an organ of the Spirit, he was not exempted from the common condition of hearing God’s word from a man’s mouth, and those who object to being taught through a human voice are not worthy to have God for their teacher. Wesley draws a gentler lesson, that fellow servants in one work of God should take pains to understand one another fully. Gill notes that Aaron was given the whole commission because he was to be the spokesman.

Ellicott explains how the elders were assembled. The Israelites under oppression still had an organisation of their own, jurisdiction attaching to the heads of tribes and chief families; the Greek version calls them the senate. Moses and Aaron had no power to convoke them, so they invited them and the elders came. Calvin sees a different necessity: so vast a multitude could not be gathered into one place, and God did not wish to contend by the clamour of a mob but by miracles breathing out His power calmly. He then presses the arrangement into a question. If slowness of speech kept Moses from speaking, why was the word not addressed to Aaron in the first place? Why this circuit, by which what Moses heard directly is published only at second hand — unless the manner pleased God as a test of faith? The humility of Aaron appears in his not objecting to depend on his brother, and the tractableness of the elders in not asking why God did not address them Himself; though the miracles, Calvin allows, helped men so stupefied by misery that bare preaching would have had no weight with them. Clarke offers a plainer reason, that Aaron probably knew Hebrew better.

Ellicott finds the account very compressed: the elders heard and saw the signs first, then must have called the people together after working hours to be addressed and shown the signs. On the worship he reports and rejects the view that Moses was its object, preferring the Lord who had visited them. Gill and Clarke read the response at face value: the people credited the divine appointment, confirmed by the miracles, and bowed in thankfulness. Clarke turns the gesture into an argument about posture in prayer, describing the eastern bow that brings the head to the knees and the forehead to the ground, and remarking that those who worship at perfect ease can have no due sense of God’s majesty or their own unworthiness; let a man take the posture a criminal would before his judge. Calvin alone qualifies the belief. He takes the statement as a part standing for the whole, since the public adoration implies an assembly, and warns that this faith had no living root: it was such as the first adverse wind could scatter, and so it proved. Those who receive eagerly what is proposed in God’s name deserve no great praise unless faith is rooted deeply enough to stand under the assaults of temptation.
